clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia notable for its association with epilepsy, most often generalised tonic-clonic or complex partial seizures
Caused by a large intronic ATTCT pentanucleotide repeat expansion in ATXN10, unlike the CAG trinucleotide SCAs
Reported predominantly in individuals of Latin American (Amerindian) ancestry, an important clue in a patient with ataxia and seizures
Progressive gait and limb ataxia with dysarthria and nystagmus is the core neurological syndrome
Seizures may appear at or after the onset of ataxia and can be a prominent management issue
The expansion is very large and unstable, and anticipation may be seen across generations
Care combines supportive ataxia management with appropriate anti-seizure therapy
reference.pathophysiology: SCA10 is caused by a markedly expanded ATTCT pentanucleotide repeat located within an intron of ATXN10. Because it is non-coding, the disorder is attributed to an RNA-mediated toxic gain-of-function in which the expanded repeat transcript sequesters RNA-binding proteins and disrupts normal RNA processing, rather than to a polyglutamine protein. This leads to Purkinje cell and cerebellar cortical degeneration and, through mechanisms that remain incompletely understood, a lowered seizure threshold in many patients. The large, unstable expansion accounts for variable repeat size, anticipation and the strong founder effect observed in Amerindian-derived populations.
additionalDifferentials: Other autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxias, particularly SCA2 which can also feature seizures
Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (ataxia with epilepsy and other features)
Mitochondrial disorders combining ataxia and seizures
additionalInvestigations: Electroencephalography to characterise seizure type and guide therapy
MRI brain to document cerebellar atrophy and exclude structural lesions
Broad SCA repeat-expansion panel when ATXN10 testing is negative
Nerve conduction studies to assess for associated neuropathy
Screening for acquired ataxia causes when the picture is atypical
redFlags: Status epilepticus or poorly controlled seizures requiring urgent management
Rapid neurological deterioration suggesting an alternative or superimposed process
Prominent myoclonus and cognitive decline raising suspicion of a progressive myoclonic epilepsy
New focal deficits indicating a structural lesion rather than SCA10 alone
reference.prognosis: SCA10 generally progresses slowly over years to decades; seizure control is achievable in most patients and, when adequate, ataxia remains the main determinant of long-term disability. Prognosis is more guarded in those with frequent seizures or additional systemic features.
pitfalls: Ordering only CAG-based SCA panels and missing the pentanucleotide ATXN10 expansion
Overlooking ancestry as a diagnostic clue in a patient with combined ataxia and epilepsy
Attributing seizures to an unrelated epilepsy syndrome and delaying genetic diagnosis
Assuming all dominant SCAs share the same molecular mechanism when counselling about recurrence
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Control seizures with antiepileptic drug therapy tailored to generalised tonic-clonic and complex partial seizures and guided by EEG
Provide symptomatic ataxia care with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, gait aids and speech and language therapy, as no disease-modifying treatment exists
Manage swallowing safety with assessment and diet modification as bulbar features develop
Monitor progression of ataxia and seizure frequency, adjusting antiepileptics to maintain adequate control
Coordinate care between neurology and epilepsy services, and note Latin American Amerindian ancestry when evaluating the family
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance, the unstable expansion and anticipation across generations
